title: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The curve of growth for length or stature in man indicates a rapid increase at the outset, that is to say during the quick growth of babyhood; a long period of slower, but still rapid and almost steady growth in early boyhood; as a rule a marked quickening soon after the boy is in his teens, when he comes to “the growing age”

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Rate of growth in man”. Scope: humans, birth to adulthood

fields.label: Assessment

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The variables and phases are standard, with large public datasets covering the relevant ages. Standard spline or growth-curve analyses can decisively assess the empirical pattern within days.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit age-specific height and height-velocity curves from longitudinal or repeated cross-sectional measurements from birth to adulthood. The claimed sequence is confirmed by an infant peak, slower childhood interval, adolescent acceleration and approach to zero velocity, and refuted if those phases are absent.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: National examinations and international growth standards record stature by age in very large samples, and velocity is obtained from them by ordinary smoothing. The four-phase pattern is specific enough to fail if the adolescent quickening is absent. Population differences in timing are a real caveat, but they do not prevent a direct confirmation or refutation of the stated sequence.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Plot stature velocity against age from birth to adult height. The claim is confirmed by high infantile velocity, a lower and nearly steady childhood velocity, a distinct acceleration in the early teens, and a decline to zero at adult height. A single smooth peak, or no adolescent acceleration, would refute that phasing.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The original description was drawn largely from boys.

Populations differ in the age of the adolescent peak, so one universal calendar age is too strict.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: The population median stature-velocity curve from birth to 20 years shows, in order: a very high velocity in infancy, a lower and nearly steady velocity through childhood, a distinct rise (adolescent spurt) in the early-to-mid teens, and a fall toward zero by the end of the teens.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Downloaded NHANES DEMO and BMX files for the six 2007-2018 cycles, merged on SEQN, kept examined persons under 20 years with a stature measurement (recumbent length below 24 months, standing height from 24 months; n = 23551, boys 12038, girls 11513). For each sex, median stature by completed year of age gave the model-free yearly velocity v(a); a local-linear Gaussian-kernel smoother (SD 0.5 yr; 0.75 and 1.0 yr as sensitivity) on monthly medians gave the smoothed velocity curve on a monthly grid. Bootstrap over individuals (1000 resamples) gave 95% CIs for the infancy velocity, the adolescent excess over childhood velocity and the velocity at 18.5-19.5 yr. The four pre-registered sub-criteria were evaluated on boys and reported for girls.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered, evaluated on boys (the subject of Thompson's sentence) with girls reported alongside. Velocities come from pooled NHANES 2007-2018 measured stature (recumbent length < 24 months, standing height >= 24 months) using exam age in months. Model-free yearly velocity v(a) = median(height | age in [a+1,a+2) yr) - median(height | age in [a,a+1) yr), a = 0..18; smoothed velocity = derivative of a weighted smoothing spline through monthly medians. All four must hold for boys: (a) infancy: v(0) >= 2 x mean of v(4..9); (b) childhood steadiness: coefficient of variation of the smoothed velocity over ages 4-10 < 0.15 and max-min of v(4..9) <= 2.0 cm/yr; (c) adolescent quickening: max smoothed velocity in ages 10-17 >= 1.2 x the minimum smoothed velocity in ages 6-10, and the largest v(a) for a in 10..16 exceeds mean v(4..9) by >= 1.0 cm/yr with a 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples of individuals) excluding 0; (d) arrest: v(18) (18.5 -> 19.5 yr) < 1.5 cm/yr and < one third of mean v(4..9).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refutes if (c) fails in boys, i.e. the adolescent peak does not exceed childhood velocity (bootstrap CI of the excess includes 0 or the smoothed ratio < 1.0), or if (a) fails (infancy velocity not above childhood velocity). Any other combination of failed sub-criteria (e.g. an irregular childhood plateau or incomplete arrest by 19.5 yr) gives 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: cm/yr (boys' adolescent peak yearly velocity minus mean childhood velocity, ages 4-10)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's 'curve of growth for length or stature' and its phases are read as the first derivative (velocity, cm/yr) of median stature against age. NHANES is cross-sectional, so the population-median velocity is a smoothed version of individual velocity: the adolescent spurt is attenuated and widened relative to longitudinal curves, which makes criterion (c) conservative. 'Babyhood' is taken as the first two years, 'early boyhood' as 4-10 years, 'teens' as 10-17, 'full height' as 19-20 years. Birth length is not in NHANES, so infancy velocity is measured from the 0-11 month to the 12-23 month median (midpoints ~0.5 and ~1.5 years).

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
NHANES Demographic Variables and Sample Weights (DEMO), cycles 2007-2008 to 2017-2018

NHANES Body Measures (BMX), cycles 2007-2008 to 2017-2018

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Deviation from pre-registration: the pre-registered 'weighted smoothing spline' derivative on monthly medians was numerically unstable (adjacent-year smoothed velocities swung between 2.7 and 13.8 cm/yr), so the smoothed velocity uses a fixed-bandwidth (SD 0.5 yr) local-linear Gaussian-kernel smoother on the same monthly medians; thresholds were not changed. Results at bandwidths 0.75 and 1.0 yr are reported and give the same sub-criterion outcomes for boys.

Criterion (b) is met at the threshold: the range of boys' yearly velocities between ages 4 and 10 is exactly 2.0 cm/yr (allowed <= 2.0), driven by a pre-pubertal dip to 4.7 cm/yr at 8.5-9.5 yr. Childhood velocity in boys declines slowly (7.6 -> 4.8 cm/yr smoothed, ages 3-9) rather than being flat; 'nearly steady' holds only relative to infancy and adolescence.

Cross-sectional data: population medians attenuate and spread the adolescent spurt; in girls the spurt (peak 10.9 yr) is so attenuated that its excess over childhood velocity (0.9 cm/yr) has a bootstrap CI including 0, so criterion (c) fails for girls even though the pattern is visible. Thompson's sentence is about boys, which is why the verdict is scored on boys.

Birth length is absent from NHANES, so 'infancy' velocity is measured between the 0-11 and 12-23 month medians (about 14 cm/yr), which understates the true first-year velocity.

Modern US population (2007-2018), not the 19th-century European boys Thompson drew on; timing of the spurt differs between populations but the sequence of phases is what was tested.
